item.title: Can One Ancient Hum Really Awaken the Pineal Gland?
item.description: By age forty, there's a seventy percent chance your pineal gland has started calcifying. By fifty-five, it's over eighty percent. Yet an ancient yogic technique called Brahmari — just three minutes of daily humming — may reverse this. Researchers at the Karinolinska Institute found that humming increases nitric oxide production fifteen-fold, and that molecule can reach the pineal gland through the cribriform plate to dissolve calcified deposits. The same mechanism cardiologists have used for decades to clear arterial plaque, applied to the most enigmatic gland in the human brain.

item.title: Why Georgia Is Considered the Cradle of Civilisation
item.description: The country of Georgia yields some of the most extraordinary archaeological discoveries in human history. From 1.8 million year old Homo erectus skulls at Dmanisi — the oldest hominin fossils found outside Africa — to the world's earliest wine production dating back 8,000 years, the Shulaveri-Shomu culture's pioneering agriculture, the wealthy kingdom of Colchis that inspired the myth of Jason and the Golden Fleece, and one of only fourteen independent alphabets on Earth. Georgia is not merely a chapter in the story of civilisation — it may well be the prologue.

item.title: Anthropic Engineer Shows How to Give AI Agents Real Memory
item.description: An Anthropic engineer demonstrates a three-layer architecture for giving AI agents genuine persistent memory. Memory stores act as a file system that attaches to sessions, supporting versioning and per-user configuration. The dreaming process runs asynchronously in the background, using a multi-agent system to fact-check, enrich, consolidate, and organise stored information without destroying the originals. With an expected ninety-five percent cache hit rate and three composable layers — sessions, memory stores, and dreaming — this fundamentally changes what AI agents can remember across conversations.

item.title: Karpathy on Software 3.0: Vibe Coding, Verifiability, and What Remains Human
item.description: Andrej Karpathy traces the evolution from Software 1.0 through 2.0 to 3.0 — where prompting replaces programming and the context window becomes your primary lever. He explains why AI capabilities are jagged rather than uniform, why verifiability is the key to building with AI, and how vibe coding democratises creation while agentic engineering raises the ceiling. The animals versus ghosts analogy reframes what these systems actually are, and the parting lesson is clear: you can outsource your thinking, but you cannot outsource your understanding.

item.title: The Anarchist Who Tried to Destroy Marx's Movement
item.description: Mikhail Bakunin was born into Russian nobility and discarded every privilege for revolutionary activism. Karl Marx believed the working class should seize the state; Bakunin believed the state itself was the trap. Their rivalry inside the International Working Men's Association ended with Bakunin's expulsion at the 1872 Hague Congress after Marx weaponised a blackmail letter from a third party. The International collapsed within four years. A century later, Bakunin's warning — that revolutionaries who inherit state machinery become the new tyrants — was borne out across every Marxist revolution of the twentieth century.

item.title: Subqueue Claims 52x Faster Long-Context AI With Sub-Quadratic Attention
item.description: A Miami-based startup called Subqueue claims to have built a model with a 12 million token context window using Sub-Quadratic Sparse Attention, or SSA. Rather than attending to every token, the model skims the query, decides which tokens matter, and only attends to those, turning a quadratic cost problem into a linear one. The company says it runs 52 times faster than Flash Attention at one-fifth the cost. But there are no published technical reports, no independent verification, and no benchmarks for the headline 12 million token claim. With former Meta and Google engineers on the team, the pedigree is there but the evidence is not — yet.

item.title: Mises Media: Rothbard's Political Strategy as Entrepreneurship
item.description: After Thomas Massie's defeat in the most expensive House primary in U.S. history, the Mises Institute panel discusses what went wrong and what libertarians should do next. Ryan McMaken, Connor O'Keeffe, and Tho Bishop explore how Rothbard treated political strategy as entrepreneurship — with scarce time and resources governed by opportunity cost. They question the value of libertarian congressmen in modern DC, examine the generational divide between young Massie supporters and older Fox News viewers, and propose alternative approaches including state-level activism and building special interest groups for liberty.

item.title: The Narcissist State: A Psychological Perspective on Statism
item.description: What if the State operates not through ideology but through the precise dynamics of narcissistic abuse? Philip Bodessell, a UK barrister imprisoned for refusing COVID masking, maps family roles like Golden Child, Enabler, and Scapegoat onto political structures and identifies mechanisms like Gaslighting, DARVO, and Intermittent Reinforcement in statecraft. The framework is structural, not conspiratorial, and aims to give people a compass and map for concrete exit strategies rather than abstract philosophical arguments.

item.title: Kinsella vs Rose: The Libertarian Civil War Over Intellectual Property
item.description: Stefan Kinsella dissects Larken Rose's arguments against intellectual property — and finds Rose guilty of the very hypocrisy he denounces. Rose opposes copyright on principle, yet issued DMCA takedowns when his own film was pirated. Kinsella argues that property rights only apply to scarce, rivalrous resources, that creation itself does not confer ownership, and that once information escapes into the world, third parties have no contractual obligation to its creator. A philosophical cage match between two libertarians who agree on almost everything except this.

item.title: This Home Costs $300 to Build and $0 to Heat FOREVER. Why Is It Banned?
item.description: Adobe — just mud, sand, and straw — outperforms modern construction in strength, insulation, and cost, yet it's been systematically excluded from building codes for nearly a century. Each brick costs three cents, walls maintain stable temperatures without any mechanical system, and a University of Arizona study showed adobe homes needed zero cooling while wood-frame homes ran air conditioning ten months a year. The codes were written by the Portland Cement Association, an $18 billion industry protecting its market. But legal loopholes exist, and Simone Swan used them to build 600 adobe homes for families earning under $12,000 a year — with zero energy bills and no mortgage.

item.title: What the Founding Fathers of Israel Actually Said Behind Closed Doors
item.description: Historical documents and statements from Israel's own founding figures paint a more complicated picture than the standard narrative suggests. Ben-Gurion called partition a temporary strategy. Weizmann said it would only last 25 to 30 years. The same patterns of contested narratives and resistance to scrutiny echo into the present, shaping how we see the conflict today.
